text: Hello, I'm Lena Pertzelmaier, and I'm working
at Senckenberg in Frankfurt, Germany, and I'm part of the
Biodiversity Meets Data Project,
for which I will present today their workflows and how they
fit into the European biodiversity data space.
So I want to start with an example that we use a lot in BMD, which
is where we have two stakeholders.
On the one side, we have a scientist, and the scientist, in this
case, an ecologist, for example, develops a really good species
distribution model for predicting where a species might occur
today and also in the future with changing climate.
And on the other side, we have a Natura 2000 site manager,
which are the main stakeholders in BMD.
And those site managers, they want to understand how a
certain invasive species may expand within their conservation
area. So there's a clear link between the scientist and the
Natura 2000 site manager, and the Natura 2000 site manager
would really benefit from having a way
to reuse and access the model
outputs that the scientists produce.
So the question is, how can this be achieved?
And this is where the workflow engine that we've developed comes in.
So the first step that the scientist needs to take
is an obvious one. They would need to share their code.
So that actually enables others to inspect the code, and if they are
skilled enough, they can also try to reuse it.
But obviously, this often leads to troubles because we also need to
have the right environment and the right dependencies installed.
That's why we don't only want the scientists to publish their code, but also, you
guessed it, containerize it.
So that way, the model becomes portable and executable.
But that's not enough to actually understand how the model is working.
If the model has different steps that need to follow each other, we need to know
that.
We also need to know which inputs are required for the model to run, and we
also would like to know beforehand which outputs are produced.
This is why we also require the scientist to define a
workflow. Workflows basically consist of
defining inputs, steps, and outputs.
There are many different workflow specifications that can be used for
this task. In BMD, we mainly work with Argo, but
have also considered the common workflow language.
But the important part is no matter which workflow specification you use, it
usually also comes with a workflow runner that can actually execute
your workflow. And those workflow runners, they can also
run on remote infrastructure. So actually, if you have
access to a remote
execution infrastructure that supports the workflow language,
the site managers don't need to run the
workflows and the model on their local machines anymore, which might have
very limited hardware specs,
but they can actually easily run the model on a
remote machine.
So now we have something like this, where the Natura 2000 site
manager can submit a workflow to a workflow engine, and then
once the workflow engine finished, he receives the
workflows back and has the results.
But this process is still missing very important information.
So the workflow itself does not have any license information, so we don't even know
if we are allowed to reuse the workflow.
We also don't have an author attribution
or things like descriptions and keywords to understand what the workflow is
about. We also don't know in which workflow language this
workflow specification is written, and thus, if our
workflow engine is actually able to execute the model.
And this is where
metadata comes in, and in our case, we went for the Workflow
RO-Crate profile to describe the workflows that have been developed.
The main entity that has been introduced for that is the
computational workflow,
which basically describes the script
that describes the workflow, which is also part of the Workflow RO-Crate.
And this computational workflow is then again described by many other
entities, such as the creator, or which programming
language, and also it defines the inputs that are required
and the outputs that are expected.
So this way of looking at a workflow is also called the
prospective provenance. It is a way of looking at the workflow
before it is initiated or before it is executed.
It's a kind of a general workflow description,
like a recipe that has not yet been executed.
But we also want to have a way how to describe workflows that have actually been
run and that have produced results.
And for that, we use the workflow run RO-Crate profile, which is
basically an extension of the workflow RO-Crate profile, as you can
see, and it adds as a main entity this create action,
which references the computational workflow.
It also specifies an agent which
triggered this execution, and it specifies
the objects, which are the values that
are used as an input parameter. So for example, if the
formal parameter, the input, says species name,
this object, this property value, then defines exactly
for which species this workflow has run.
And last but not least, obviously it also contains information
about the results that have been produced, which you can also see here because
this workflow RO-Crate
now also contains an
outputs folder with all the generated files.
So in total, our workflow engine architecture looks
like this. So in the middle of it sits the RO-Crate service, which
connects user interfaces, workflow engines, and workflow registries.
And the flow is basically that the user interface
submits a workflow RO-Crate to the RO-Crate service, which then
unpacks the workflow manifest and submits that to a workflow engine.
Once the workflow has been executed, the RO-Crate receives the workflow run
information and uses that to package it again into a
workflow run RO-Crate. This run RO-Crate is
then fed back to the user interfaces and can also be published
on different workflow registries.
As you can see, we have multiple user interfaces and multiple workflow
engines deployed. One implementation is Workflow.earth,
which is deployed in Destination Earth, where also the workflow engine
sits. And it was our first implementation of a workflow
engine
focusing on agricultural digital twins.
And on the other side, we have the BMD BAT platform.
And
the workflow engine for this BAT platform is deployed
at our BMD partner, LifeWatch ERIC.
And as you can see, there are different workflow registries to which the
workflows can be published, such as, for example, the BMD
DataSpace, Workflow Hub, or Workflow.earth.
So now I want to show you our implementation of Workflow.earth,
where you can see here now a detailed view of a
workflow that has been run. You can see that it contains
standard information,
the title, description, and so on.
And it also contains provenance information, so when was the workflow triggered,
with which parameters, and so on. All of this information comes from
the workflow run RO-Crate, which is rendered in a human-readable way
here on this web page of Workflow.earth.
So for a human, this is quite clear what this web page is about, but the thing
is, a machine arriving at this page has no idea what it is about
without having to go into the page itself and try to
analyze that.
This is why FAIR Signposting has been developed.
FAIR Signposting basically provides information to machines
already in the HTTPS header,
and it contains information like
what is this page even about? Is there some information that
describes this in a closer way? What is the license of this page,
who authored it, and so on.
Usually, this signposting information is not visible to the user
browsing on the web page, but you can actually
visualize the signposting by using a signposting sniffer, at least in the
Chrome browser.
So what we have developed actually on Workflow.earth is that we
combine a unique identifier that gives each workflow a clear
identity
with RO-Crates that package the workflow, the metadata, the provenance,
and so on,
and FAIR Signposting, which makes information
easy to find on the web also for machines.
And
with all of that, we actually are able to expose those workflow
runs as W3C FAIR Digital Objects, which means we can
provide the workflow information and all the details that
belong to this workflow in a both human-readable and also in a
machine-actionable way.
So lastly, I want to show you the user interface that is being
developed in BMD.
It has the same
back end as the Workflow.earth platform,
but it is being developed with the special needs and requirements that the
Natura 2000 stakeholders have.
So basically, you can go to the page and browse the different workflows that are
available,
and then once you select a workflow, you can define the different
parameters in an
interactive way. So you can select the species that you're interested in from a
drop-down list, you can select the area you're interested in on the map
directly, and then you can submit the workflow.
The workflow then goes to the LifeWatch ERIC workflow engine.
And once it is finished, it produces also this kind of dashboard that you can see
here on the right side, which enables The Natura 2000
site manages to directly browse the results in the browser
without having to even download them.
But of course, we also offer them the
possibility to download the results in form of a workflow run
RO-Crate, which then contains all the files, and they can
do with those files whatever they want.
So that being said,
what have we developed to summarize?
So we
focus very much on workflows that are really fair, and we
enforce this also with the workflow engine by
using a standard workflow language and enforcing
that the data also comes with the right metadata, which then
makes the workflows portable, reproducible, and reusable.
We focus also a lot on federated data infrastructures because we
really want to be able to connect to multiple workflow registries and to multiple
workflow execution engines
so the workflows can be shared and reused across institutions.
And we focus on web-fair digital objects by combining
the unique identifier, the RO-Crate, and fair signposting to make
workflows and workflow runs discoverable, citable, machine
actionable on the web.
That's all from my side. I want to thank all the BMD project partners and thank you
